question: Will Auyl win the second most seats in the 2026 Kazakh Kurultai elections?
rules:
Parliamentary elections to elect the Kurultai of Kazakhstan are scheduled to take place on August 23, 2026.

This market will resolve to the political party that wins the second-most number of seats in the Kurultai of Kazakhstan as a result of this election.

If the results of the specified election are not definitively known by July 31, 2027, this market will resolve to "Other".

The named parties will be primarily ranked by the number of seats won in the specified election. If two or more parties are tied on seats, ties will be broken by the total number of valid votes received, with higher vote totals ranking higher. If parties remain tied, ties will be broken by alphabetical order of the listed party names. This market will resolve to the party that occupies the second finishing position after applying this ranking.

This market's resolution will be based solely on the number of seats won by the named party.

This market will resolve based on the results of the elections, as indicated by a consensus of credible reporting. In the case of ambiguity, this market will resolve solely based on the results as reported by the Kazakh government.

evidence.publisher: AnewZ — opinion by Nurbolat Nyshanbayev, Assistant Professor, Turan University
evidence.excerpt: On 23 August, Kazakhstan will vote for the Kurultai, a new 145-seat, single-chamber parliament. Its deputies will be elected entirely through national party lists, with a 5% threshold for representation and no constituency races or independent candidates. Adilet enters the race with the strongest organisational position after absorbing Amanat in June. Auyl has centred its campaign on rural Kazakhstan, food security, land reform and protections for agricultural workers.

evidence.publisher: The Times of Central Asia — Andrei Matveev
evidence.excerpt: Three national surveys place Adilet first and Auyl second ahead of the August 23 election. The Institute of Eurasian Integration interviewed 4,000 respondents face-to-face from July 16 to 26, reporting a margin of error no greater than 1.54%. It recorded Adilet at 65.1%, Auyl at 5.9%, Ak Zhol at 4.7%, Respublica at 4.6%, the NSDP at 4.2% and the People’s Party at 4.1%. An earlier DATAmetrics survey of 8,000 respondents recorded Auyl at 7.3%, ahead of Ak Zhol at 4.6% and Respublica at 3.4%.

The Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development conducted a nationwide telephone survey of 1,200 respondents from July 8 to 20, 2026. Adilet received 64.8% support, Auyl 5.4%, Respublica 4.8% and Ak Zhol 4.7%. Auyl’s rural support was about 1.5 times its urban support. Another 10.9% of respondents remained undecided, while 2.2% intended to vote against all parties.

evidence.publisher: Central Election Commission of the Republic of Kazakhstan
evidence.excerpt: As of July 23, 2026, the lists of the seven political parties contesting seats in the Kurultai included a total of 545 candidates. The participating parties included Auyl. The election of deputies of the Kurultai was scheduled for August 23, 2026.

evidence.publisher: Central Election Commission of the Republic of Kazakhstan
evidence.excerpt: The Central Election Commission registered Auyl’s party list for the Kurultai election scheduled for August 23, 2026. Auyl nominated 69 individuals, all of whom were found to meet constitutional and electoral-law requirements. The commission recalled that Auyl received 10.90% of the vote in the previous Mazhilis election, exempting it from the electoral deposit.

evidence.publisher: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights
evidence.excerpt: The last parliamentary elections were held early on March 19, 2023, with six of seven registered parties entering the Majilis. Amanat received 62 seats, Auyl eight, Ak Zhol and Respublika six each, the People’s Party five and the National Social-Democratic Party four; independent candidates won seven seats. Previous ODIHR reports noted that the political landscape was strongly dominated by the ruling party and that the distinction between the party and the executive branch was often blurred.
